components.text: Whether publicly testable scientific mechanisms exhaust every meaningful or genuine explanatory question.
Whether the success and mutual support of scientific ideas establish an unlimited explanatory scope.
The decisive completeness claim is answered by identifying meaningful questions outside natural science.
The claim that scientific mechanism exhausts rational explanation is opposed by agency and purpose explanations.
Whether purported nonmechanistic or historical explanations are rationally warranted rather than merely meaningful questions.
The proposed legitimacy of wider historical or divine explanation is challenged through testimony quality and bodily decay.
Whether ordinary natural regularities and bodily decay logically exclude a resurrection attributed to exceptional agency.
Whether the available historical testimony is sufficiently credible to warrant belief in the alleged exception.
Whether scientific laws can delimit all rational claims about exceptional agency.
Natural laws describe regular events and therefore cannot by themselves exclude an exceptional agent-caused resurrection.
The testimony-quality objection remains a separate historical evidential demand.
Whether agency or purpose genuinely explains anything alongside a mechanistic account.
Whether invoking exceptional divine agency adds explanatory content to a claimed miracle.
The claim that agency adds explanation is challenged as a substitute for investigating operative natural processes.
The possibility of exceptional agency is not directly defeated merely by demanding an underlying mechanism.
Whether scientific inquiry can account for and warrant trust in the rational faculties on which its method depends.
Whether theism supplies explanatory content rather than merely stopping investigation.
The reliability presupposed by scientific evidence is challenged under a mindless and unguided origin of cognition.
Theism is offered as a foundation for rational trust rather than as a replacement for scientific investigation.
Whether evolution can produce cognitive faculties capable of reliable and extraordinary scientific understanding.
Whether mathematical success remains possible where unaided human intuition is limited.
The claimed unreliability of evolved faculties is opposed by their demonstrated capacity for extraordinary understanding.
Limits of intuition are distinguished from the continuing precision of mathematical prediction.
What best explains the fit between an intelligible universe, mathematics, and minds capable of scientific understanding.
Whether scientific method can explain its own rational and historical preconditions.
The fit between an intelligible universe and scientific minds is offered a creator-based cumulative explanation.
The fact of evolved cognitive achievement is accepted but argued to have a deeper explanatory ground.
Whether questions of cosmic purpose identify an objective explanatory demand or project human concerns onto reality.
Whether a rational creator provides evidence of an ultimate purpose for the universe.
Purpose questions are challenged as extrapolations from temporary human purposes rather than features of the universe.
The creator explanation is indirectly opposed by denying evidence of cosmic purpose.
Whether natural law requires a rational personal source to explain its existence and structure.
A specified impersonal account of natural laws is offered against the need for a rational agent behind them.
Whether an impersonal account removes the explanatory need for a nonphysical source behind the universe.
Whether a nonphysical creative source is compatible with established scientific findings about a cosmic beginning.
The demand for a non-agent origin is answered by distinguishing no physical material from absolute nothing.
Divine mind is asserted as the creative source of the universe and its law-governed beginning.
Whether cosmic origin requires a nonphysical divine mind rather than an impersonal zero-balance process.
Whether an intelligible ordered universe requires a rational personal source.
A natural origin from balanced opposites is offered against the inference from cosmic beginning to divine mind.
Zero total charge and energy are invoked to motivate a universe arising without a creator.
Whether theistic belief is evidentially insulated or can be revised by counterexplanations and defeaters.
Whether historical counterevidence could rationally defeat the resurrection commitment.
The charge of unrevisable supernatural belief is answered by identifying historical and experiential defeaters.
Challenges to Gospel authenticity and resurrection history are admitted as potentially belief-revising.
Whether an evolutionary and consequence-based description of moral behavior supplies prescriptive duties or merely describes facts.
Describing evolved conduct and consequences does not by itself derive prescriptive duties or ethical foundations.
Whether scientific progress and evolution already explain the origin of life rather than only changes after life exists.
Whether evolutionary explanation has domain conditions that limit what it can establish.
Evolution cannot supply the origin-of-life case because natural selection presupposes already living replicating systems.
The evolutionary account of morality after life exists is not directly disputed by this origin boundary.
